intro: Welcome to creative writing! In C2 reading you learnt to spot a narrator, imagery and show, don't tell in other people's stories, and in the style lesson you learnt to control rhythm and voice. Now you write your own scenes: a narrator with a clear voice, details only your story has, dialogue that sounds like real people, and feelings the reader sees without being told.
teachingNotes: Build on the chain and recap each in one line, don't re-teach: c2-reading-literary (narrator: first person, third person, omniscient, unreliable; show, don't tell and imagery as READING concepts), c2-figurative-language (simile, metaphor, mixed metaphors) and c2-stylistic-nuance (adjusting style and tone, controlling rhythm and word choice for a consistent voice). Earlier: b1-writing-stories-articles (story shape, past tenses, short sentences instead of 'and … and …') and b2-narrative-tenses. New here: the learner WRITES fiction and description. COPYRIGHT: every extract in the lesson is an original practice text; you may name famous writers or books, but never quote real literature beyond a few words. Write new examples in the style needed.

distinctive-voice: voice = how the writing sounds: who tells it, what they notice, the words they choose. Choose a narrator and keep it: first person (I: close, but only knows what 'I' sees and thinks), close third person (follows one character's thoughts), omniscient (knows everyone's thoughts); don't jump into another character's head by accident. Tense: the past simple is the standard for stories; the present gives immediacy (common in modern fiction and in jokes told aloud); both are fine, switching by accident is not. Indonesian verbs don't mark time, so tense slips are the typical error ('She opened the door and sees her brother'); a flashback with had + past participle or a fact that is still true is not a slip. Specific sensory detail, using sound, smell and touch as well as sight: not 'The market was busy' but what you hear, smell and see in Pasar Beringharjo ('Monggo, Mbak!', cloves, dried teri, a buruh gendong). Precise verbs and nouns instead of adverb/adjective + general word (walked slowly → shuffled; looked at → stared at / glanced at; ate quickly → wolfed down; a car → a dented Avanza). Vary rhythm: a short sentence after long ones hits hard. Avoid clichés (as white as snow, her heart skipped a beat, time stood still, at the end of the day) and purple prose (over-decorated writing: adjective piles, adverbs everywhere, a metaphor in every line). Indonesian habit: long adjective chains ('pasar yang ramai, indah, unik, dan menakjubkan' → 'busy, colourful, vibrant and amazing'): choose one precise detail instead.

natural-dialogue: layout and punctuation: quotation marks (British books usually single '…', American double "…"; Indonesian uses double; either is fine if consistent); punctuation inside the closing mark; before a speaker tag a full stop becomes a comma and the tag starts with a small letter ('I'm tired,' she said.); ? and ! stay ('Ready?' he asked.); a tag before the words takes a comma and the speech a capital (Budi said, 'Let's go.'); a split tag has commas on both sides; a new paragraph for each new speaker. 'said' (and 'asked' for questions) is the default, almost invisible tag; fancy tags (exclaimed, articulated, retorted, opined) and adverbs (said angrily) pull attention and tell the feeling. Action beats instead of tags: a separate sentence with a full stop ('I'm fine.' Rina pushed her plate away.), never a comma before a non-speech verb. How people talk: contractions, fragments and short answers, interruptions with a dash, trailing off with an ellipsis, avoiding the question, not explaining what both know ('As you know, Budi, we have been married for ten years' is written only for the reader). Every line should reveal character or move the story. Realistic, not a transcript: leave out most ums and ers. Indonesian habit: textbook dialogue in bahasa baku ('Apakah kamu sudah makan siang?') with full sentences and names in every line, which sounds stiff in English; formal speech is right only for characters who really talk that way.

show-dont-tell: the node's common error: 'She was very sad.' → 'She stared at the unopened letter until her tea went cold.' Show through actions and habits, the body, objects, dialogue and what a character avoids saying; the reader works the feeling out and feels it more. Indonesian habit: naming the emotion and intensifying it ('hatinya sangat sedih sekali' → 'her heart was very, very sad'): intensifiers don't add feeling, details do. Telling is right for summary, transitions and time jumps ('Three years passed.'), background and minor details: show the moments that matter, tell the bits in between. After showing, don't explain it again (no 'She was very sad.' after the cold tea).

Limits: no new grammar (every structure is available at C2; the point is control and choice). Don't teach poetry and metre, screenwriting, plot structure theory or publishing. Much of creative writing is taste: in the learner's free writing, praise the voice first, then correct one or two clear things only (a tense slip, a dialogue punctuation error, a cliché, a fancy tag, a named emotion at a key moment). Test only clear cases: one answer clearly better for the stated purpose. Typed answers: accept synonyms of the right idea (anxious / worried / nervous); an answer in Indonesian shows understanding, but ask for the English word.

keyPoints.title: A distinctive voice: narrator, tense and specific detail
keyPoints.explanation: Choose a narrator (first person I, close third person, or omniscient) and keep it. Write in one tense: the past simple is the standard for stories, the present gives immediacy; don't switch by accident. Describe with specific sensory detail (what you hear, smell, see and touch) and precise verbs and nouns instead of piles of adjectives. Vary the rhythm, and cut clichés and purple prose (over-decorated writing).

examples.en: I knew the shop was closing before Pak Hasan did.
examples.id: Aku sudah tahu toko itu akan tutup sebelum Pak Hasan tahu. (orang pertama: dekat, tetapi hanya tahu apa yang 'aku' tahu)

examples.en: A batik seller called 'Monggo, Mbak!' over the scrape of a broom.
examples.id: Seorang penjual batik berseru 'Monggo, Mbak!' di antara bunyi sapu yang menggesek lantai. (detail bunyi yang spesifik)

examples.en: Dimas wolfed down his nasi goreng.
examples.id: Dimas melahap nasi gorengnya. (kata kerja yang tepat, bukan 'ate quickly')

id.title: Suara yang khas: narator, tense dan detail yang spesifik
id.explanation: Pilih narator (orang pertama I, orang ketiga yang mengikuti satu tokoh, atau serba tahu) dan pertahankan. Menulislah dalam satu tense: past simple adalah standar untuk cerita, present terasa lebih langsung; jangan berpindah tanpa sengaja. Gambarkan dengan detail indrawi yang spesifik (apa yang kamu dengar, cium, lihat dan sentuh) dan kata kerja serta kata benda yang tepat, bukan tumpukan kata sifat. Variasikan ritme kalimat, dan buang klise serta purple prose (tulisan yang terlalu dihias).

keyPoints.title: Dialogue that sounds natural
keyPoints.explanation: Put the spoken words in quotation marks, with the punctuation inside; before a speaker tag, a full stop becomes a comma ('I'm tired,' she said). Start a new paragraph for each new speaker. Use said (asked for questions) as the default tag, or an action beat instead of a tag. Real people use contractions, short answers and interruptions, avoid questions and never explain what both of them already know. Every line should show who the person is or move the story.

examples.id: 'Aku nggak lapar,' kata Budi. (koma sebelum tag, bukan titik)
'Udah makan?' 'Di kantor.' (pendek, seperti orang sungguhan bicara)

examples.en: 'I'm fine.' Rina pushed her plate away.
examples.id: 'Aku baik-baik saja.' Rina mendorong piringnya menjauh. (action beat: tindakan menggantikan tag, dan menunjukkan perasaannya)

id.title: Dialog yang terdengar alami
id.explanation: Taruh kata-kata yang diucapkan di dalam tanda petik, dengan tanda bacanya di dalam; sebelum speaker tag (keterangan siapa yang bicara), titik berubah jadi koma ('I'm tired,' she said). Mulai paragraf baru setiap kali pembicaranya berganti. Pakai said (asked untuk pertanyaan) sebagai tag bawaan, atau action beat (tindakan) sebagai pengganti tag. Orang sungguhan memakai bentuk singkat (contractions), jawaban pendek dan saling memotong, menghindari pertanyaan, dan tidak pernah menjelaskan hal yang sudah sama-sama mereka ketahui. Setiap baris sebaiknya menunjukkan siapa orangnya atau menggerakkan cerita.

keyPoints.title: Show, don't tell (and when to tell)
keyPoints.explanation: Telling names the feeling (She was very sad); showing gives the evidence and lets the reader feel it: actions, the body, objects, dialogue and what a character avoids saying. Intensifiers like very and extremely don't add feeling; details do. Telling is still right for summary and transitions: show the moments that matter, tell the bits in between, and don't explain a feeling after you've shown it.

examples.en: She stared at the unopened letter until her tea went cold.
examples.id: Dia menatap surat yang belum dibuka itu sampai tehnya dingin. (menunjukkan kesedihan tanpa menyebut kata 'sad')
Tiga tahun berlalu. (memberi tahu itu tepat untuk lompatan waktu)

id.title: Show, don't tell (dan kapan boleh memberi tahu)
id.explanation: Telling (memberi tahu) menyebut perasaannya (She was very sad); showing (menunjukkan) memberi buktinya dan membiarkan pembaca merasakannya: tindakan, tubuh, benda, dialog dan hal yang dihindari seorang tokoh untuk dikatakan. Kata penguat seperti very dan extremely tidak menambah perasaan; detail yang menambahnya. Telling tetap tepat untuk ringkasan dan peralihan: tunjukkan momen-momen yang penting, ceritakan saja bagian di antaranya, dan jangan menjelaskan perasaan yang sudah kamu tunjukkan.

guidedPractice.prompt: Choose the more precise verb for an old man with a bad knee: 'Pak Darto ___ to the gate.' (walked slowly / shuffled)
guidedPractice.hint: One verb already contains the 'slowly' and the tiredness.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which of these is a cliché that a story should cut: 'time stood still' or 'the clock above the counter kept ticking'?
guidedPractice.hint: Which phrase have you read in a hundred stories already?

guidedPractice.prompt: In a story, Rina speaks, and then Budi answers. Does Budi's line go in the same paragraph as Rina's, or in a new paragraph?
guidedPractice.hint: How does the reader know who is talking without a tag on every line?

guidedPractice.prompt: Which feeling does this sentence show? 'Budi read the message, laughed out loud on the empty train, and read it again.' Choose one: happy, scared, bored.
guidedPractice.hint: What do people do when they laugh out loud and read a message twice?

independentPractice.prompt: This first-person story suddenly jumps into the third person: 'I pushed open the door of my kos. She was too tired to cook.' Which pronoun should replace 'She'?
Which sentence is the action beat in this line? 'Of course I'm happy for her.' Sari deleted the photo.
independentPractice.hint: Which sentence shows what Sari does instead of telling us who spoke?

independentPractice.prompt: Which sentence shows that Bu Ani is tired? A: 'Bu Ani was very tired.' B: 'Bu Ani fell asleep with her glasses still on.' Write A or B.
independentPractice.hint: Which one names the feeling, and which one lets you see it?

assessment.prompt: Read this practice text (an original extract written for this lesson). 'In the hospital corridor, Dimas turned his phone over and over in his hands. Every time the ward doors opened, he stood up, then sat down again.' The text never names the feeling. Which feeling does it show? Choose one: bored, anxious, proud, angry.
assessment.rubric: Correct: anxious (worried and nervous have the same idea = 100): he can't keep his hands still and stands up every time the doors open, waiting for news. 'scared' or 'afraid' = 70 (close, but anxious fits the waiting better). 'bored' = 0 (bored people don't jump up at every door). 'proud' or 'angry' = 0 (nothing in the actions supports them). The idea in Indonesian ('cemas', 'gelisah') = 50: ask for the English word.

assessment.prompt: This line from a story draft has one punctuation mistake: 'I'll be home late tonight.' said Sari. Which punctuation mark should replace the full stop after 'tonight'? Write its name in one word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: comma: when a speaker tag (said Sari) follows the spoken words, the full stop becomes a comma inside the quotation mark: 'I'll be home late tonight,' said Sari. 'question mark' or 'exclamation mark' = 0 (the line isn't a question or an exclamation). 'quotation mark' = 0 (that's already there). The corrected line written out with the comma = 100. The idea in Indonesian ('koma') = 50: ask for the English word.

assessment.prompt: A writer wants a speaker tag that readers hardly notice, so that the spoken words stay in focus. Choose one word to complete the line: 'The last train has gone,' Pak Hasan ___. (exclaimed, articulated, said, declared)
assessment.rubric: Correct: said: it's the default tag, almost invisible, so the reader looks at the words, not the writing. 'exclaimed' = 0 (it needs an exclamation and pulls attention to itself). 'articulated' or 'declared' = 0 (fancy tags: they sound written, not spoken). 'told' = 0 (told needs a person: told his wife). An action beat instead of a word = 50: correct idea, but the question asks for the tag.

assessment.prompt: This sentence from a story draft has one cliché (a phrase used so often that readers no longer notice it). Write the cliché: 'Bu Ani left the house at the crack of dawn, with a basket of salak on her arm and her late husband's umbrella.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: at the crack of dawn (= very early in the morning, a worn-out phrase; a fresh version would use a detail, e.g. 'before the first adzan'). 'a basket of salak' or 'her late husband's umbrella' = 0: these are the specific, fresh details that make the sentence good. Only 'dawn' = 50 (the right place, but write the whole phrase).

assessment.prompt: A writer moves quickly from one scene to the next: 'The next two years were quiet. Sari finished her degree and moved to Surabaya.' Is this passage showing or telling? Write one word.
assessment.rubric: Correct: telling: it sums up two years in two sentences without a scene. That is the right choice here: telling is for summary and transitions, so the story can get to the next moment that matters. 'showing' = 0 (no actions, objects or dialogue let the reader work anything out). 'telling' with the comment that it's wrong here = 70 (the label is right, but telling is fine for a transition). The idea in Indonesian ('memberi tahu') = 50: ask for the English word.

assessment.prompt: This story is told in the past tense, but one verb slips into the present. Write that verb in the correct past form: 'The rain stopped just after midnight. Rina locked the shop, pulled her jacket tighter and walks to the bus stop on Jalan Malioboro.'
assessment.rubric: Correct: walked: stopped, locked and pulled are in the past simple, so the third verb in the list must be too (walks is a tense slip, common because Indonesian verbs don't change for time). 'walks' = 0 (that's the mistake). 'was walking' = 50 (past, but it breaks the list of single completed actions). The whole sentence rewritten with 'walked' = 100.

assessment.prompt: In a story, Budi's friend asks where Rina is. Rewrite Budi's answer as people really say it, using contractions: 'I do not know. I have not seen her since Monday.'
acceptableAnswers: i don't know i haven't seen her since monday
i don't know i've not seen her since monday
don't know i haven't seen her since monday
don't know haven't seen her since monday
i dunno i haven't seen her since monday
dunno i haven't seen her since monday
dunno haven't seen her since monday
no idea i haven't seen her since monday
no idea haven't seen her since monday
assessment.rubric: Correct: I don't know. I haven't seen her since Monday. (I've not seen her is also fine, more British; dropping I in 'Don't know' or 'Haven't seen her' is natural in casual speech.) Only one of the two contractions = 50. No contractions = 0 (that's the stiff original). Changing the meaning (e.g. 'I saw her on Monday') = 20. Missing apostrophes when typed (dont, havent) = 90: right idea, mention the spelling.

material.title: Your voice: choosing a narrator and a tense

blocks.text:
**Quick recap:** in C2 reading you learnt to *spot* a narrator, imagery and *show, don't tell* in other people's stories; in the style lesson you learnt to control rhythm, word choice and a consistent voice. Now you *write*. Your **voice** is how your writing sounds: who is telling the story, what they notice and which words they choose. It starts with two decisions.
- **Who tells the story?** A **first-person narrator** (*I*) feels close and personal, but can only know what *I* sees, hears and thinks. A **close third-person narrator** (*she*, *he*) follows one character and knows only that character's thoughts. An **omniscient narrator** (all-knowing) knows everyone's thoughts: powerful, but harder to make feel close. Choose one and **keep it**: don't suddenly jump into another character's head.
- **Which tense?** The **past simple** is the standard for stories in English (*Rina locked the shop and ran for the bus*). The **present** (*Rina locks the shop. The bus is already pulling away.*) gives a feeling of **immediacy**, as if it's happening right now: it's common in modern fiction and when people tell a funny story aloud. Both are fine. What's not fine is **switching** in the middle of a scene without a reason.

id.text:
**Rekap singkat:** di pelajaran membaca C2 kamu belajar *mengenali* narator, citraan (imagery) dan *show, don't tell* di cerita orang lain; di pelajaran gaya kamu belajar mengatur ritme, pilihan kata dan suara tulisan yang konsisten. Sekarang kamu *menulis*. **Voice** (suara penulis) adalah cara tulisanmu terdengar: siapa yang bercerita, apa yang dia perhatikan dan kata apa yang dia pilih. Semuanya dimulai dari dua keputusan.
- **Siapa yang bercerita?** **Narator orang pertama** (*I*, aku-an) terasa dekat dan pribadi, tetapi hanya bisa tahu apa yang dilihat, didengar dan dipikirkan si *I*. **Narator orang ketiga yang dekat** (*she*, *he*) mengikuti satu tokoh dan hanya tahu isi pikiran tokoh itu. **Narator serba tahu** (omniscient) tahu isi pikiran semua orang: kuat, tetapi lebih sulit terasa dekat. Pilih satu dan **pertahankan**: jangan tiba-tiba masuk ke kepala tokoh lain.
- **Tense apa?** **Past simple** adalah standar untuk cerita dalam bahasa Inggris (*Rina locked the shop and ran for the bus*). **Present** (*Rina locks the shop. The bus is already pulling away.*) memberi kesan **langsung**, seolah-olah terjadi saat ini juga: ini umum di fiksi modern dan ketika orang menceritakan kisah lucu secara lisan. Dua-duanya boleh. Yang tidak boleh adalah **berpindah** di tengah adegan tanpa alasan.

rows.en: I knew the shop was closing before Pak Hasan did.
rows.id: Aku sudah tahu toko itu akan tutup sebelum Pak Hasan tahu.
rows.note: first person: close, but only what 'I' knows

id.note: orang pertama: dekat, tetapi hanya tahu apa yang 'aku' tahu

rows.en: Rina read the email twice. Two floors up, her manager had already forgotten sending it.
rows.id: Rina membaca email itu dua kali. Dua lantai di atasnya, manajernya sudah lupa pernah mengirimnya.
rows.note: omniscient: the narrator knows what Rina can't know

id.note: serba tahu: narator tahu hal yang tidak mungkin diketahui Rina

rows.en: Rina locks the shop. The last bus is already pulling away.
rows.id: Rina mengunci toko. Bus terakhir sudah mulai berangkat.
rows.note: present tense: immediate, as if it's happening now

id.note: present tense: terasa langsung, seolah sedang terjadi sekarang

rows.en: Rina locked the shop, but the last bus was already pulling away.
rows.id: Rina mengunci toko, tetapi bus terakhir sudah mulai berangkat.

id.note: past tense: pilihan standar

blocks.text:
**The Indonesian trap: tense slips.** Indonesian verbs don't change for time (*kemarin dia pergi*, *besok dia pergi*), so in a long story the past tense easily slips back into the present: *She opened the door and sees her brother.* After you write, read **only the verbs**: are they all in the same tense? A flashback with *had* + past participle (*she had left Bandung years before*) or a fact that is still true (*Yogyakarta is in Java*) is not a slip.
**Rhythm is part of your voice.** Mix long sentences with short ones. A short sentence after two long ones hits hard. *She waited.*

id.text:
**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: tense yang tergelincir.** Kata kerja bahasa Indonesia tidak berubah karena waktu (*kemarin dia pergi*, *besok dia pergi*), jadi dalam cerita yang panjang past tense mudah tergelincir kembali ke present: *She opened the door and sees her brother.* Setelah menulis, baca **kata kerjanya saja**: apakah semuanya dalam tense yang sama? Kilas balik dengan *had* + past participle (*she had left Bandung years before*) atau fakta yang masih benar (*Yogyakarta is in Java*) bukan kesalahan.
**Ritme adalah bagian dari suaramu.** Campur kalimat panjang dengan kalimat pendek. Kalimat pendek setelah dua kalimat panjang terasa menghantam. *She waited.*

blocks.prompt: A story is written in the past tense. Which sentence keeps the tense consistent?
options: Dimas paid for the coffee and leaves without his change.
Dimas paid for the coffee and left without his change.
Dimas pays for the coffee and left without his change.
blocks.explain: Both verbs must be in the past simple: **paid** and **left**. The other two mix past and present in one sentence, the typical slip when your first language doesn't mark tense.

id.prompt: Cerita ditulis dalam past tense. Kalimat mana yang tense-nya konsisten?
id.explain: Kedua kata kerjanya harus past simple: **paid** dan **left**. Dua kalimat lainnya mencampur past dan present dalam satu kalimat, kesalahan khas kalau bahasa ibumu tidak menandai tense.

material.title: Specific detail, precise words, no clichés

id.title: Detail spesifik, kata yang tepat, tanpa klise

blocks.text:
**Specific beats general.** *The market was busy* tells the reader nothing they couldn't guess. A writer with a voice shows what **this** market is like: what you **hear**, **smell**, **see** and **touch**. Use more than sight: sound and smell bring a place to life fastest.
**Precise verbs and nouns do the work** of adjectives and adverbs:
- *walked slowly* → *shuffled* (old, tired) or *strolled* (relaxed); *looked at* → *glanced at* (quickly) or *stared at* (for a long time); *ate quickly* → *wolfed down*.
- *a flower* → *a frangipani*; *a car* → *a dented Avanza*; *some food* → *a plate of gudeg*.
**Clichés** (klise) are phrases used so often that readers no longer see them: *as white as snow*, *her heart skipped a beat*, *time stood still*, *at the end of the day*. Replace them with a detail only your story has.
**Purple prose** is over-decorated writing: piles of adjectives, adverbs everywhere, a metaphor in every line. The name comes from an old Latin image of a bright purple patch sewn onto plain cloth. It sounds as if the writer is trying too hard, and the reader stops seeing the scene.

id.text:
**Yang spesifik mengalahkan yang umum.** *The market was busy* tidak memberi tahu pembaca apa pun yang belum bisa mereka tebak. Penulis yang punya suara menunjukkan seperti apa pasar **yang ini**: apa yang kamu **dengar**, **cium**, **lihat** dan **sentuh**. Jangan hanya penglihatan: bunyi dan bau paling cepat menghidupkan sebuah tempat.
**Kata kerja dan kata benda yang tepat melakukan tugas** kata sifat dan kata keterangan:
- *walked slowly* → *shuffled* (berjalan terseret-seret: tua, capek) atau *strolled* (berjalan santai); *looked at* → *glanced at* (melirik sekilas) atau *stared at* (menatap lama); *ate quickly* → *wolfed down* (melahap).
- *a flower* → *a frangipani* (bunga kamboja); *a car* → *a dented Avanza* (Avanza yang penyok); *some food* → *a plate of gudeg*.
**Klise** (clichés) adalah frasa yang terlalu sering dipakai sampai pembaca tidak lagi memperhatikannya: *as white as snow*, *her heart skipped a beat*, *time stood still*, *at the end of the day*. Ganti dengan detail yang hanya dimiliki ceritamu.
**Purple prose** (prosa ungu) adalah tulisan yang terlalu dihias: tumpukan kata sifat, kata keterangan di mana-mana, metafora di setiap baris. Namanya berasal dari gambaran Latin kuno tentang tambalan ungu terang yang dijahit di kain polos. Tulisannya terdengar terlalu berusaha, dan pembaca berhenti melihat adegannya.

rows.en: The market was busy and full of interesting things.
rows.id: Pasarnya ramai dan penuh barang menarik.

id.note: umum: pembaca tidak melihat apa-apa

rows.en: The incredibly busy, colourful, vibrant, noisy, magical market was a breathtaking rainbow of endless wonders.
rows.id: Pasar yang luar biasa ramai, berwarna-warni, semarak, bising dan ajaib itu adalah pelangi keajaiban tanpa akhir yang memukau.
rows.note: purple prose: five adjectives, still no picture

id.note: purple prose: lima kata sifat, tetap tidak ada gambaran

rows.en: At Beringharjo, a batik seller called 'Monggo, Mbak!' over the scrape of a broom.
rows.id: Di Beringharjo, seorang penjual batik berseru 'Monggo, Mbak!' di antara bunyi sapu yang menggesek lantai.
rows.note: specific: a sound (monggo = Javanese for 'please, come in')

id.note: spesifik: bunyi (monggo = bahasa Jawa untuk 'silakan')

rows.en: Near the spice stalls, the air smelled of cloves, turmeric and dried teri.
rows.id: Di dekat kios rempah, udaranya berbau cengkih, kunyit dan teri kering.

id.note: spesifik: bau

rows.en: A buruh gendong climbed the stairs with a sack of shallots tied to her back in a faded jarik.
rows.id: Seorang buruh gendong menaiki tangga dengan sekarung bawang merah yang diikat di punggungnya dengan jarik yang sudah pudar.
rows.note: specific: a person only this market has

id.note: spesifik: sosok yang hanya ada di pasar ini

blocks.text:
**The Indonesian habit: adjective chains.** Indonesian descriptions often stack adjectives: *pasar yang ramai, indah, unik, dan menakjubkan*. In English, a list like *busy, colourful, vibrant and amazing* sounds empty, because every word is general. Choose **one precise detail** instead of four adjectives. (British *colourful*, American *colorful*.)
**Not every simile is a cliché, but many are tired.** *As busy as a bee* is fine in conversation (you met it in the figurative language lesson), but in a story it's worn out. A fresh comparison comes from your own world: *as quiet as a bank on Lebaran morning*.

id.text:
**Kebiasaan bahasa Indonesia: rantai kata sifat.** Deskripsi bahasa Indonesia sering menumpuk kata sifat: *pasar yang ramai, indah, unik, dan menakjubkan*. Dalam bahasa Inggris, daftar seperti *busy, colourful, vibrant and amazing* terdengar kosong, karena setiap katanya umum. Pilih **satu detail yang tepat** daripada empat kata sifat. (*colourful* ejaan Inggris Britania, *colorful* ejaan Amerika.)
**Tidak semua simile itu klise, tetapi banyak yang sudah usang.** *As busy as a bee* tidak masalah dalam percakapan (kamu sudah bertemu dengannya di pelajaran bahasa kiasan), tetapi dalam cerita ungkapan itu sudah aus. Perbandingan yang segar datang dari duniamu sendiri: *as quiet as a bank on Lebaran morning* (sesepi bank di pagi Lebaran).

blocks.prompt: Which sentence describes a kos room with the most specific detail?
options: My room was small, simple and quite uncomfortable.
My room was so small that I could open the window without getting out of bed.
My tiny, cramped, narrow, miserable room was a sad prison of loneliness.
blocks.explain: The second sentence gives one concrete picture that proves how small the room is. The first is general, and the third is **purple prose**: four adjectives and a heavy metaphor, but we still can't see the room.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang menggambarkan kamar kos dengan detail paling spesifik?
id.explain: Kalimat kedua memberi satu gambaran konkret yang membuktikan betapa kecilnya kamar itu. Kalimat pertama umum, dan kalimat ketiga adalah **purple prose**: empat kata sifat dan metafora yang berat, tetapi kita tetap tidak bisa melihat kamarnya.

material.title: Dialogue that sounds like real people

id.title: Dialog yang terdengar seperti orang sungguhan

blocks.text:
**Dialogue on the page.** Four rules:
- **Quotation marks** go around the spoken words. British books usually use single marks ('…'), American books double ("…"). Either is fine: choose one and keep it.
- **Punctuation goes inside** the closing mark. If a **speaker tag** (the words that say who's talking, like *she said*) follows, a full stop becomes a **comma**, and the tag starts with a small letter: *'I'm tired,' she said.* A question mark or an exclamation mark stays: *'Are you coming?' he asked.* If the tag comes first, put a comma after it and start the speech with a capital: *Budi said, 'Let's just order.'*
- **A new paragraph for each new speaker**, even if they say only one word. That's how the reader knows who's talking without a tag on every line.
- **said** is the default tag (and **asked** for questions). Readers hardly notice it, so the words stay in focus. Fancy tags (*exclaimed*, *articulated*, *retorted*, *opined*) and adverbs (*said angrily*) pull attention to the writing, and they usually *tell* the feeling instead of showing it.
**Action beats.** Instead of a tag, show what the speaker does: *'It's not my fault.' Dimas put the broken mug on the table.* The beat is a **separate sentence**, so the spoken words end with a full stop, not a comma (*put* is not a way of speaking). A beat tells us who's speaking AND how they feel.

id.text:
**Dialog di halaman.** Empat aturan:
- **Tanda petik** mengapit kata-kata yang diucapkan. Buku Inggris Britania biasanya memakai petik tunggal ('…'), buku Amerika petik ganda ("…"). Dua-duanya boleh: pilih satu dan pertahankan.
- **Tanda baca masuk ke dalam** tanda petik penutup. Kalau setelahnya ada **speaker tag** (keterangan siapa yang bicara, seperti *she said*), titik berubah jadi **koma**, dan tag-nya dimulai dengan huruf kecil: *'I'm tired,' she said.* Tanda tanya atau tanda seru tetap: *'Are you coming?' he asked.* Kalau tag-nya di depan, beri koma setelahnya dan mulai ucapannya dengan huruf kapital: *Budi said, 'Let's just order.'*
- **Paragraf baru untuk setiap pembicara baru**, walaupun dia hanya mengucapkan satu kata. Dengan begitu pembaca tahu siapa yang bicara tanpa tag di setiap baris.
- **said** adalah tag bawaan (dan **asked** untuk pertanyaan). Pembaca hampir tidak memperhatikannya, jadi fokusnya tetap pada kata-katanya. Tag yang mewah (*exclaimed*, *articulated*, *retorted*, *opined*) dan kata keterangan (*said angrily*) menarik perhatian ke tulisannya, dan biasanya *memberi tahu* perasaannya, bukan menunjukkannya.
**Action beat (tindakan pengganti tag).** Daripada tag, tunjukkan apa yang dilakukan pembicaranya: *'It's not my fault.' Dimas put the broken mug on the table.* Beat itu **kalimat tersendiri**, jadi ucapannya diakhiri titik, bukan koma (*put* bukan cara berbicara). Beat memberi tahu siapa yang bicara SEKALIGUS bagaimana perasaannya.

rows.id: 'Kalau kamu terlambat,' kata Bu Ani, 'kami mulai tanpa kamu.'

id.note: tag di tengah: koma di kedua sisinya

rows.note: a tag before the words: comma, then a capital letter

id.note: tag sebelum ucapan: koma, lalu huruf kapital

blocks.text:
**How people really talk.** Real speech is short, messy and indirect:
- **Contractions** (bentuk singkat): *I'm, don't, it's, you'll*. *I do not know* sounds like a robot, or a very angry person.
- **Fragments and short answers**: *'Eaten yet?' 'At work.'*
- **Interruptions** with a dash (—), and **trailing off** with three dots (…): *'I was only going to—' 'I know what you were going to do.'*
- **Not saying everything**: people avoid the question, change the subject, answer with another question. What they don't say is often the point.
- **Not explaining what both people already know.** *'As you know, Budi, we have been married for ten years'* is there only to inform the reader: no wife says this to her husband. Let the facts come out naturally, or put them in the narration.
Good dialogue sounds real but isn't a transcript: leave out most *um*s and *er*s. Every line should **show who the person is** or **move the story**, ideally both.

id.text:
**Cara orang sungguhan berbicara.** Ucapan sungguhan itu pendek, berantakan dan tidak langsung:
- **Contractions** (bentuk singkat): *I'm, don't, it's, you'll*. *I do not know* terdengar seperti robot, atau orang yang sedang sangat marah.
- **Potongan kalimat dan jawaban pendek**: *'Eaten yet?' 'At work.'*
- **Saling memotong** ditandai tanda pisah (—), dan **kalimat yang menggantung** ditandai tiga titik (…): *'I was only going to—' 'I know what you were going to do.'*
- **Tidak mengatakan semuanya**: orang menghindari pertanyaan, mengganti topik, menjawab dengan pertanyaan lain. Yang tidak dikatakan sering justru intinya.
- **Tidak menjelaskan hal yang sudah sama-sama diketahui.** *'As you know, Budi, we have been married for ten years'* (Seperti kamu tahu, Budi, kita sudah menikah sepuluh tahun) ditulis hanya untuk memberi tahu pembaca: tidak ada istri yang bilang begitu ke suaminya. Biarkan faktanya muncul secara alami, atau taruh di narasi.
Dialog yang bagus terdengar nyata tetapi bukan transkrip: buang sebagian besar *um* dan *er*. Setiap baris sebaiknya **menunjukkan siapa orangnya** atau **menggerakkan cerita**, idealnya keduanya.

blocks.text: **The Indonesian habit: textbook dialogue.** Dialogue in school compositions often uses formal *bahasa baku* (*Apakah kamu sudah makan siang?*), full sentences and a name or title in every line. Translated, it sounds stiff: *'Have you already eaten your lunch, Sari?' 'Yes, Mother, I have already eaten my lunch.'* Real people say *'Eaten?' 'Yeah, at work.'* Keep formal speech for characters who really talk that way (a strict official, a nervous job candidate): then it shows character.

id.text: **Kebiasaan bahasa Indonesia: dialog ala buku pelajaran.** Dialog di karangan sekolah sering memakai *bahasa baku* (*Apakah kamu sudah makan siang?*), kalimat lengkap dan nama atau sapaan di setiap baris. Kalau diterjemahkan, hasilnya kaku: *'Have you already eaten your lunch, Sari?' 'Yes, Mother, I have already eaten my lunch.'* Orang sungguhan bilang *'Eaten?' 'Yeah, at work.'* Simpan bahasa formal untuk tokoh yang memang berbicara seperti itu (pejabat yang kaku, pelamar kerja yang gugup): justru di situ bahasa formal menunjukkan karakter.

blocks.prompt: Bu Ani tells her husband some news. Which line sounds natural?
options: 'As you know, Hasan, our son Dimas moved to Surabaya three years ago, and he called today.'
'Dimas called. He's not coming for Lebaran.'
'I would like to inform you that our son will not be coming home for Lebaran.'
blocks.explain: The second line is short, uses a contraction (*He's*) and goes straight to the news. The first explains facts her husband already knows (*As you know…*), and the third is office language, not a wife talking to her husband.

id.prompt: Bu Ani menyampaikan kabar kepada suaminya. Baris mana yang terdengar alami?
id.explain: Baris kedua pendek, memakai bentuk singkat (*He's*) dan langsung ke kabarnya. Baris pertama menjelaskan fakta yang sudah diketahui suaminya (*As you know…*), dan baris ketiga adalah bahasa kantor, bukan istri yang berbicara kepada suaminya.

blocks.text: **The Indonesian habit: naming the feeling, then making it bigger.** *Hatinya sangat sedih sekali* becomes *Her heart was very, very sad*, and the reader feels nothing. Intensifiers (*very, extremely, so*) don't add feeling; details do. A quick test: if you can underline an emotion word (*sad, angry, nervous, proud*) at a key moment of your story, try replacing that sentence with what the character does.

id.text: **Kebiasaan bahasa Indonesia: menyebut perasaannya, lalu membesar-besarkannya.** *Hatinya sangat sedih sekali* menjadi *Her heart was very, very sad*, dan pembaca tidak merasakan apa-apa. Kata penguat (*very, extremely, so*) tidak menambah perasaan; detail yang menambahnya. Tes cepat: kalau kamu bisa menggarisbawahi kata perasaan (*sad, angry, nervous, proud*) di momen penting ceritamu, coba ganti kalimat itu dengan apa yang dilakukan tokohnya.

blocks.prompt: Which sentence shows that Sari is nervous before her presentation, instead of telling us?
options: Sari was extremely nervous before her presentation.
Sari felt a strong and terrible nervousness.
Sari checked the projector cable for the fourth time and forgot to drink her coffee.
blocks.explain: The third sentence gives actions as evidence (checking the cable again and again, forgetting her coffee), and we work out that she's nervous. The first two **name** the feeling and try to make it bigger with *extremely*, *strong* and *terrible*.

id.prompt: Kalimat mana yang menunjukkan bahwa Sari gugup sebelum presentasinya, bukan memberi tahu kita?
id.explain: Kalimat ketiga memberi tindakan sebagai bukti (memeriksa kabel berulang-ulang, lupa minum kopinya), dan kita sendiri yang menyimpulkan bahwa dia gugup. Dua kalimat pertama **menyebut** perasaannya dan mencoba membesarkannya dengan *extremely*, *strong* dan *terrible*.

suggestedQuestions: Can you check whether my dialogue sounds natural?
Should I write my story in the past or the present tense?
How can I show that a character is angry without using the word angry?
Can you help me describe a rainy evening in Jakarta without clichés?

id.note: Pelajaran animasi singkat dari novelis Nalo Hopkinson tentang cara menarik pembaca masuk ke cerita lewat pancaindra dan detail yang spesifik dan mengejutkan, dengan contoh dari dua penulis fiksi. Bahasa Inggris berkecepatan penutur asli; nyalakan subtitle bahasa Inggris di YouTube kalau perlu.

resources.title: Three anti-social skills to improve your writing - Nadia Kalman
resources.note: A short animated lesson on writing dialogue: the writer Nadia Kalman suggests 'anti-social' habits such as eavesdropping on real conversations, imagining your characters as real people and muttering their lines to yourself. Native-speed English.

id.note: Pelajaran animasi singkat tentang menulis dialog: penulis Nadia Kalman menyarankan kebiasaan 'anti-sosial' seperti menguping percakapan sungguhan, membayangkan tokoh-tokohmu sebagai orang nyata dan menggumamkan dialog mereka sendiri. Bahasa Inggris berkecepatan penutur asli.

resources.title: Quotation Marks with Fiction, Poetry, and Titles
resources.note: A short reference from an American university writing lab: a new paragraph for each speaker, commas around dialogue tags, and how to punctuate one character's speech across several paragraphs. It also covers quoting poetry and titles, which this lesson doesn't need.

id.note: Rujukan singkat dari pusat penulisan sebuah universitas Amerika: paragraf baru untuk setiap pembicara, koma di sekitar tag dialog, dan cara memberi tanda baca pada ucapan satu tokoh yang panjangnya beberapa paragraf. Halaman ini juga membahas cara mengutip puisi dan judul, yang tidak dibutuhkan di pelajaran ini.

id.intro: Selamat datang di menulis kreatif! Di pelajaran membaca C2 kamu belajar mengenali narator, citraan dan show, don't tell di cerita orang lain, dan di pelajaran gaya kamu belajar mengatur ritme dan suara tulisan. Sekarang kamu menulis adeganmu sendiri: narator dengan suara yang jelas, detail yang hanya dimiliki ceritamu, dialog yang terdengar seperti orang sungguhan, dan perasaan yang dilihat pembaca tanpa harus diberi tahu.
suggestedQuestions: Bisa cek apakah dialogku terdengar alami?
Sebaiknya ceritaku ditulis dalam past tense atau present tense?
Bagaimana menunjukkan bahwa seorang tokoh marah tanpa memakai kata angry?
Bisa bantu aku menggambarkan sore yang hujan di Jakarta tanpa klise?

assessment.cw-1: Baca teks latihan ini (kutipan orisinal yang ditulis untuk pelajaran ini). 'In the hospital corridor, Dimas turned his phone over and over in his hands. Every time the ward doors opened, he stood up, then sat down again.' Teks ini tidak pernah menyebut perasaannya. Perasaan apa yang ditunjukkannya? Pilih satu, dalam bahasa Inggris: bored, anxious, proud, angry.
assessment.cw-2: Baris dari draf cerita ini punya satu kesalahan tanda baca: 'I'll be home late tonight.' said Sari. Tanda baca apa yang seharusnya menggantikan titik setelah 'tonight'? Tulis namanya dalam satu kata bahasa Inggris.
assessment.cw-3: Seorang penulis ingin speaker tag (keterangan siapa yang bicara) yang hampir tidak diperhatikan pembaca, supaya fokusnya tetap pada kata-kata yang diucapkan. Pilih satu kata untuk melengkapi baris ini: 'The last train has gone,' Pak Hasan ___. (exclaimed, articulated, said, declared)
assessment.cw-4: Kalimat dari draf cerita ini punya satu klise (frasa yang terlalu sering dipakai sampai pembaca tidak lagi memperhatikannya). Tulis klisenya: 'Bu Ani left the house at the crack of dawn, with a basket of salak on her arm and her late husband's umbrella.'
assessment.cw-5: Seorang penulis berpindah cepat dari satu adegan ke adegan berikutnya: 'The next two years were quiet. Sari finished her degree and moved to Surabaya.' Apakah bagian ini showing atau telling? Tulis satu kata dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.cw-6: Cerita ini ditulis dalam past tense, tetapi satu kata kerja tergelincir ke present. Tulis kata kerja itu dalam bentuk lampau yang benar: 'The rain stopped just after midnight. Rina locked the shop, pulled her jacket tighter and walks to the bus stop on Jalan Malioboro.'
assessment.cw-7: Dalam sebuah cerita, teman Budi bertanya di mana Rina. Tulis ulang jawaban Budi seperti cara orang benar-benar mengucapkannya, dengan bentuk singkat (contractions): 'I do not know. I have not seen her since Monday.'
